title: How Rob Walling bought and revived HitTail, a dying SaaS, in 4 months
summary: Rob explains how he bought HitTail, a neglected SEO SaaS, via a cold email and escrow for far less than "dot com" pricing. He then stabilized the infrastructure and plugged funnel leaks using contractors. It also lays out his self-funded "micropreneur" philosophy over chasing VC exits.

principles.text: Aim for modest, self-funded success that makes you happy rather than the VC-backed big-exit story the tech press sells.
principles.quote: I’m all about figuring out what’s going to make a person happy and then going after that with ravenous determination, instead of pursuing what we’re told is going to make us happy by the tech press

principles.text: SEO is an unsexy but powerful channel; it can deliver targeted, high-converting traffic with ROI beating most other sources.
principles.quote: People don’t tend to talk about SEO as a sexy marketing approach, but it can generate enormous amounts of highly-targeted, high-converting traffic.

principles.text: Find acquisition targets among neglected products you already know; cold email the owner directly.
principles.quote: On a warm day in early June I cold emailed the owner through the website contact form.

principles.text: Anchor on your own valuation from experience rehabbing apps; don't pay "dot com" pricing when the owner counters high.
principles.quote: I’ve acquired many web apps in the past, and I wasn’t prepared to pay “dot com” pricing for it.

principles.text: After buying, fix infrastructure risk first, then plug funnel leaks like unended trials, missing trial emails and dead-end content pages.
principles.quote: During the trial period a user received exactly zero emails. No reminders to check out their fancy new suggestions. No inquiry as to why they never installed the code. Zip.

principles.text: Use contractors rather than employees to rebuild a product quickly, and pitch in on the code yourself.
principles.quote: And that something involved me hiring a developer and a designer to help me revamp this thing (both contractors, of course, since I don't hire employees). I also put in quite a bit of coding time myself.
